newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy left appeals for key reforms.
newsitem.headline: Italy left appeals for key reforms.

text.p: Italy's ex-communists, now the main engine of government after decades shut out of power, ended a four-day congress on Sunday calling for left and right to pull together to tackle key constitutional and welfare reforms.
Change was one of the buzzwords as more than 1,000 delegates from the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS) packed a Fascist-era sports stadium for what could well be their last gathering.

Leader Massimo D'Alema, who steered the left to its first taste of government for nearly half a century at last April's general election, now wants to relaunch the PDS in the spring with a new name and logo to consolidate its power further.
In a keynote speech to the congress on Saturday night, he appealed for courage to ensure that the left did not throw away its historic chance to lead the renewal of Italy.

But D'Alema, who heads a cross-party commission charged with outlining reforms to Italy's constitution, urged a show of "common responsibility" and generosity from the centre-right opposition to strengthen Italy's fractious political system and ensure it is in shape to help found a European single currency.

"It will be a tough challenge in the next few months but we will be with the government...to achieve it," he said. "I am convinced the country will make it if we develop a sense of common responsibility."

Relations between the centre-right Freedom Alliance and Prime Minister Romano Prodi's Olive Tree coalition have been in the spotlight at the congress as the government grapples with the twin headaches of EMU and reform of the welfare state.

Prodi told the PDS he was encouraged by overtures from Freedom Alliance leader Silvio Berlusconi on Europe. Berlusconi has offered Prodi a deal on cuts in welfare spending in return for support over budgetary measures needed to qualify for EMU.

But the government, which took office in May, came in for tough criticism at the congress from Sergio Cofferati, head of Italy's biggest trade union, CGIL, who attacked its employment policies and warned against cuts in the welfare state.
D'Alema hit back at Cofferati, accusing his union of being "deaf and closed" and said it would be marginalised if it did not adapt to the changing demands of society.
He added that the Prodi government must forge a "social pact" by reforming welfare spending to ensure that benefits were shared out more fairly.
Party delegates approved a document recommending an overhaul of "traditional" welfare policy. They also backed plans to change the electoral system and legalise light drugs.
D'Alema was overwhelmingly re-elected as party leader on Sunday after standing unopposed and was given an even greater say in how the PDS is run.
The party, which ditched communism six years ago but kept a small red hammer and sickle on its party flag, also faced changes, D'Alema said.
He wants to make it into wider social democratic force to boost its share of the vote from 21 percent last April.
The PDS hopes to unveil its new look -- which could wipe the last vestiges of communism off the party logo -- in April and newspapers say it will be called "Democratic and European Left".
